chunks: Layout guidelines for test points. The question: What are layout guidelines for test points?
Test points work only if a probe can land on them reliably. So the layout has rules about pad size, spacing, side of the board, and distance from tall parts.
The rules come from the size of the spring-loaded probes and the small errors in lining the board up. The factory's own guideline always overrides typical numbers.
Think of marked parking spaces. Each space must be big enough for the car, spaced so doors open, and kept clear of pillars.
If the spaces are too small or too close, cars scrape and miss. A test pad is a parking space for a probe.
The fixture plate is like a low ceiling: a tall part next to the pad is a pillar that blocks it. Putting all spaces on one level, the bottom, keeps the garage simple.
Pads sit on a regular grid with spacing at least the probe's receptacle size; a keep-out strip separates them from tall parts so the fixture plate can lie flat.
Ground pads (green) are scattered among signal pads (orange).
Pad: a bare copper circle, about 1 mm across, left uncovered by the green protective coating (solder mask). Pitch: the center-to-center spacing between neighboring pads.
Keep-out: space around a pad or tall part where nothing else may sit. Tooling holes: holes that align the board to the fixture.
Stub: the short spur of copper joining a pad to its net (the copper connection it tests). Ground pad: a pad on the ground net near signal pads, for a return connection.
A typical rule set: pads about 1 mm wide, centers at least 1. 27 mm apart, so the gap between neighboring pads is at least 0. 27 mm.
Keep about 1 mm away from small parts, more from tall ones, and about 3 mm from the board edge. Put every pad on the bottom and add two tooling holes at asymmetric spots.
Connect each pad straight onto its net with no stub. That is the whole idea.
"Make each test point a bare, flat pad of about a millimetre or more, on one side of the board, on a grid with at least about 1.
27 mm spacing, clear of tall parts and the edge, with tooling holes for alignment.
Connect it in-line to the net with minimal stub, put ground pads nearby, label it on the silkscreen, and check against the factory's DFT rules.
On fast nets, I keep the stub tiny or skip the pad."
